children: By Kumar Tanishk
Australian shares eked out gains on Monday as investors backed commodity-linked stocks over banks, with ANZ's margin squeeze souring sentiment toward the major lenders.
ANZ

, the country's fourth-largest lender by market capitalisation, fell 3.2% to post its weakest session in over 8 months after its net interest margin, a key profitability gauge, shrank even as annual profit rose.

The drop is a "classic sell the fact behaviour," said KCM Trade chief market analyst Tim Waterer, adding that the market had already priced in a decent margin outcome, so the numbers failed to surprise on the upside.
Financials
slipped 1.1% to mark their worst day since October 14, with the other three 'Big Four' banks down between 0.6% and 1.4%.
Top lender Commonwealth Bank of Australia
is due to report results later this week.
Despite the drag from banks, the S&P/ASX 200
edged up 0.1% to 9,029.70. Last week, the benchmark rose 1.3% — better than the United States and parts of Asia because of its low exposure to the AI names.
Australia's status as a relative safe harbour does not make the banks automatic winners when risk appetite turns, Waterer said.

"If sentiment toward the majors (banks) is deteriorating, capital is more likely to rotate into selective resources names that still offer leverage to commodities, or into defensives with clearer earnings visibility," he said.
Leading gains, miners
rose 3.1% to nearly a month high, as copper prices advanced. BHP
and Rio Tinto
gained 2.7% and 1.6%, respectively.
Gold stocks
climbed 4.2% to their higher since October 12 on higher bullion prices, while oil-linked stocks
gained 0.7%.
Bond yields firmed slightly. Australia's 10-year yield
rose to about 5% from a two-and-a-half-month low hit on Friday.
In New Zealand, the benchmark S&P/NZX 50
New Zealand faces a weeks-long wait to learn who will govern after an election that left Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's bloc clinging to a razor-thin lead.
